This guide assumes you already have a working and up-to-date Linux distribution installed, and have all the required dependencies installed in order to compile software, including wine.

Preamble

Patching Wine is not as daunting as it sounds, in fact, despite how long it took me to get around to writing this "guide", it's straight forward, and the only time sink you'll encounter is waiting for your patched version of Wine to compile, rather than hours spent resisting the urge to put your fist through your screen. So, here we go

Prerequisites

Beyond the myriad of optional dependencies used to build Wine, there are a couple of tools you will need to get started.

Git

This command line tool is used to interact with source code repositories utilizing the git protocol. You'll use this to pull down the source code and patches from the Wine Project's github repositories.

Make

Another command line tool, this one used to compile source code into a package which can be installed. Can also be used to install compiled source code by use of the install command.

Patch

Yet another command line tool, this one is used to apply changes stored in a .patch file.

Grab Vanilla Wine

In order to add custom patches to Wine, you'll first need the un-compiled source code of the base Wine project, which can be obtained from the following repository:

git://source.winehq.org/git/wine.git

To download, crack open your favourite terminal emulator and enter the following lines:

mkdir /path/to/where/you/want/to/store/the/source/code

cd /path/to/where/you/want/to/store/the/source/code

git clone git://source.winehq.org/git/wine.git

Run the configure script

Within the main directory of the source tree you just downloaded will be a configure shell script. This needs to be run to prepare the source code for compiling and to generate the makefile which is used by the make command in a later step to generate the installable package.

In the terminal, cd into the folder which contains the configure shell script and run it by entering:

./configure

If you plan to build a 64bit aware version of wine, you'll need to pass the --enable-win64 flag to the configure script, like so:

./configure --enable-win64

Watch the output of the script carefully, as it will provide you with a list of missing dependencies at the end. If there is anything critical missing, the script will not complete successfully. If it does, but still shows missing dependencies, these are optional and will not prevent you from successfully compiling wine.

Check any missing dependencies for any features you know you'll want included and install them using your chosen distro's package management method, after which, run the configure script again to see if it is no longer showing as a missing dependency.

Grab the Wine Staging Patches (optional)

Wine-Staging is simply vanilla wine which has had a bunch of additional changes (patches) applied to it. While this is entirely optional, and you could go ahead and apply whatever extra patch you require directly onto vanilla wine, if you are creating a custom patched version of wine with the expressed intent of using it for gaming, you'll often want to include the staging patches as well.

To grab these patches, you'll need to download the source tree for Wine-Staging and save them into a temp directory.

mkdir /path/to/where/you/will/store/wine-staging

cd /path/to/where/you/will/store/wine-staging

git clone git://github.com/wine-staging/wine-staging

Copy the contents into your Vanilla-Wine folder.

Once you have successfully downloaded the Wine-Staging source tree, copy the entire contents into the vanilla wine folder, choosing to Merge folders and Replace files when you are prompted to do so.

Apply the Wine-Staging Patches

You should now have a patches folder in your Vanilla-Wine directory, inside of which will be the patch install shell script. You'll need to execute this shell script, with the -all flag, to install all of the patches contained within the patches folder.

cd into/the/folder/which/contains/the/patches/folder

./patches/patchinstall.sh DESTDIR="/path/to/your/vanilla-wine/folder" --all

You'll see a readout of every patch as it is applied. Once completed, you can move on to applying any other individual patches you require before attempting to compile the patched version of wine.

Applying individual patches using the patch command

Let's face it, as good as Wine-Staging is, some games require tiny tweaks to get them working, which are not included in Wine-Staging, either because they are obscure, or break other games when applied. Whatever the reason, you can apply such "third party" patches using the patch command.

Obtain the .patch file or, failing that, the raw contents of the changes which make up your patch.

Save your .patch file wherever you like, or if making your own .patch file, create a blank document with a .patch extension, and paste the copied raw changes into the file and save it.

Next, from the terminal, execute the following command, making sure your current directory is your custom wine folder:

patch -p1 < /path/to/your/.patch/file

If successful, you should see output referring to the number of file and changes made.

Compile Wine

Okay, you're now ready to compile (make) your custom wine package.

From the terminal - making sure your current working directory is the top folder of your custom wine location - execute the command:

make -j%

Note: Replace % with a numerical value equal to the number of threads your CPU has available, or the number of threads you are willing to allow to be used. For example, if you have a quad core CPU with hyper/multi-threading, you would enter: make -j8. This will greatly speed up the process of compiling.

Using your Custom-Wine Package

All things being in your favour, you should now have a compiled and custom version of wine to use in your prefixes. Now all that remains is to install it, which can be achieved in two ways.

Install as replacement for default wine

This is not recommended, as this version of wine is your distros default wine installation, and replacing it will ensure all wine prefixes, unless configured otherwise, will attempt to execute windows programs using this custom-wine install. If you're confident that this custom-wine will work, then you can replace the default wine install of your distro by doing the following:

sudo make install

Your wine install will be placed in your home folder under a hidden folder named: .wine.

Install to custom location

To install your custom-wine package to a separate location, where it will not interfere with the default system wine install, and can be invoked for specific prefixes without impacting others, simply execute:

make DESTDIR=/where/you/want/to/place/the/install install

Conclusion

And there you go, one custom wine install, which can now be invoked to run windows applications inside prefixes.

To use this custom-wine install as a Lutris runner, simply copy the folders within the "local" directory into the following location:

home/{your-username}/.local/share/lutris/runner/wine

Simply create a folder within the wine folder and launch Lutris. You'll see your custom wine available as a wine runner.
